item.text: I’m reading the highest-yield documents in this wave: the Novaya/RFE/Meduza items on LGBT repression, protest policing, and the Chechnya attack, plus the official TASS/Kremlin/legal texts as attribution context. That gives me enough to separate accepted evidence from context or duplicates.

**New Accepted Records**

- `3B-S085` [Not Gonna Get Us](https://novayagazeta.eu/en/articles/2023/12/05/not-gonna-get-us-en) | Novaya Gazeta Europe | 2023-12-05 | source type: local-language analysis | source confidence: high, because it directly ties the 2023 Supreme Court ruling to broader state-sponsored homophobia and concrete enforcement effects | final evidence use: historical arc plus immediate post-ruling LGBT fear and criminalization context | language: en | locator: `turn1view0` lines 40-41, 105-111 | factual claims: the Supreme Court declared the “international LGBT public movement” extremist; LGBT symbols may trigger fines or arrests; bookshops removed queer literature; platforms took down related content; clubs and rights groups shut down | temporal fit: strong, because it covers the 30 Nov 2023 ruling and its immediate aftermath | ruler attribution: Supreme Court, Justice Ministry, police, and the broader Putin system | inherited/context limits: analysis format, but the concrete claims are tightly anchored to the target period | contrary considerations: the article is interpretive and historical, so use the concrete enforcement details rather than the broader narrative tone | lenses: 3B.3, 3B.5, 3B.7, 3B.8

- `3B-S086` [Russia blocks 23 ‘LGBT propaganda’ websites as requested by Safe Internet League](https://novayagazeta.eu/en/articles/2023/02/10/russia-blocks-23-lgbt-propaganda-websites-as-requested-by-safe-internet-league-en-news) | Novaya Gazeta Europe | 2023-02-10 | source type: local-language reporting | source confidence: high, because it gives a dated block action, named institutions, and the number of affected sites | final evidence use: censorship and early-2023 LGBT suppression | language: en | locator: `turn1view1` lines 32-38, 44-46 | factual claims: 23 LGBT-related links were blocked; Coming Out and other resources were affected; the Safe Internet League pushed for 113 blocked sites; Roskomnadzor and Rosmolodezh were involved | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: Roskomnadzor, Rosmolodezh, Safe Internet League, and the broader regulatory apparatus | inherited/context limits: this is a blocking incident, not a full legal history | contrary considerations: mostly one-sided reporting, but the block count and named actors are concrete | lenses: 3B.3, 3B.5, 3B.8

- `3B-S087` [Russian man arrested after fellow Moscow metro passenger calls police over pictures ‘discrediting army’ in his phone](https://novayagazeta.eu/en/articles/2023/03/18/russian-man-arrested-after-fellow-moscow-metro-passenger-calls-police-over-pictures-discrediting-army-in-his-phone-en-news) | Novaya Gazeta Europe | 2023-03-18 | source type: local-language reporting | source confidence: high, because it documents a specific arrest, charge, and detention sequence with official court involvement | final evidence use: speech-policing, informant culture, and punitive detention | language: en | locator: `turn1view2` lines 32-36 | factual claims: Yuri Samoylov was arrested for pictures on his phone that “discredit the Russian army”; police acted after a passenger reported him; he received 14 days’ custody for extremist materials | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: police, courts, and the anti-war speech regime | inherited/context limits: one case, but highly illustrative of broader repression | contrary considerations: the reporting is narrow and case-specific, so it supports pattern evidence rather than by itself proving nationwide scale | lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.5, 3B.8

- `3B-S088` [Editor-in-Chief of Novaya Gazeta Europe Kirill Martynov slapped with police report in Russia for failing to mark himself as ‘foreign agent’](https://novayagazeta.eu/en/articles/2023/04/06/editor-in-chief-of-novaya-gazeta-europe-kirill-martynov-slapped-with-police-report-in-russia-for-failing-to-mark-himself-as-foreign-agent-en-news) | Novaya Gazeta Europe | 2023-04-06 | source type: local-language reporting | source confidence: high, because it identifies the enforcement basis and the official registration action | final evidence use: foreign-agent regime enforcement against media | language: en | locator: `turn1view3` lines 32-35 | factual claims: Kirill Martynov was reported for failing to label his output as required for “foreign agents”; the case entered official records and was set for court hearing | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: Justice Ministry, police, and court system | inherited/context limits: administrative enforcement example rather than direct physical violence | contrary considerations: the case is procedural on its face, but it still demonstrates coercive control and chilling effects | lenses: 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.8

- `3B-S089` [Novaya Gazeta journalist Elena Milashina and lawyer Alexander Nemov attacked in Chechnya](https://meduza.io/en/feature/2023/07/04/the-latest-cruel-act-of-intimidation) | Meduza | 2023-07-04 | source type: reputable reporting | source confidence: high, because it includes direct eyewitness/human-rights-lawyer testimony and detailed injuries | final evidence use: political intimidation, violence against a journalist and lawyer, and Chechnya impunity context | language: en | locator: `turn2view0` lines 16-25, 50-59, 70-72 | factual claims: Milashina and Nemov were beaten by masked assailants in Chechnya; the attack was linked to their work on a sensitive case; the interviewee described constant surveillance and the climate becoming scarier for journalists and rights defenders | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: Chechen local authorities/security environment, with relevance to federal tolerance and failure to restrain | inherited/context limits: regional case, not a clean national command-order record | contrary considerations: the source is interview-driven, but the attack and injuries are concretely described | lenses: 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.9, 3B.10

- `3B-S090` [Putin signs foreign agents bill into law](https://tass.com/russia/1094953) | TASS | 2017-12-03 | source type: official/state media | source confidence: medium-high for existence and text of the law, lower for benign framing | final evidence use: historical legal baseline for the foreign-agent control architecture | language: en | locator: `turn3view0` lines 111-115 | factual claims: foreign agents can include individuals and legal entities; the Ministry of Justice registers them; they must mark publications; websites can be blocked for violations | temporal fit: historical context, not target-year specific | ruler attribution: Russian federal executive and legislature under Putin | inherited/context limits: off-period baseline, useful for explaining the 2023 enforcement environment | contrary considerations: state-media framing is self-justifying, so use the legal text and enforcement powers, not the rhetoric | lenses: 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.8

- `3B-S092` [Putin signs law totally banning LGBT propaganda](https://tass.com/politics/1545959) | TASS | 2022-12-05 | source type: official/state media | source confidence: medium-high for legal text, lower for the state’s justificatory framing | final evidence use: statutory baseline for the 2023 LGBT crackdown | language: en | locator: `turn3view2` lines 113-125 | factual claims: Putin signed a law completely banning propaganda of nontraditional sexual relations, gender reassignment, and pedophilia; the ban covers social networks, media, films, and ads; internet monitoring and blocking authority were expanded | temporal fit: pre-target-year baseline, but directly drives 2023 enforcement | ruler attribution: Putin, Duma, media watchdog, and executive enforcement apparatus | inherited/context limits: this is the legal foundation, not a post-enforcement case file | contrary considerations: state-media framing calls it family protection, but the law is explicitly sweeping and punitive | lenses: 3B.3, 3B.5, 3B.7, 3B.8

- `3B-S093` [Ban on foreigners owning large classifieds websites in Russia comes into force](https://tass.com/russia/1582951) | TASS | 2023-03-01 | source type: official/state media | source confidence: medium-high for the legal restriction itself, lower for the routine-regulation framing | final evidence use: administrative control over online speech/commerce and liability exposure | language: en | locator: `turn8view1` lines 110-114 | factual claims: a ban on foreign citizens owning large classifieds websites took effect; the law was signed by Putin; violations can trigger criminal, administrative, or other liability | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: Putin and federal regulatory bodies | inherited/context limits: more of a control-and-liability example than a core violence case | contrary considerations: the article frames it as commercial regulation, but it still shows coercive administrative governance | lenses: 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.8

- `3B-S094` [Putin Signs Law Banning Gender-Reassignment Surgery, Hormonal Therapy](https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-gender-reassignment-banned-putin-signs-law/32517157.html) | RFE/RL | 2023-07-24 | source type: wire / analysis | source confidence: high, because it directly states the law’s effect and cites the Kremlin-era conservative turn | final evidence use: trans-targeting legal change and vulnerability evidence | language: en | locator: `turn4view0` lines 129-130 | factual claims: Putin signed a ban on gender-reassignment surgery and hormone therapy, with only narrow congenital-anomaly exceptions; lawmakers justified it with “family values” rhetoric | temporal fit: direct target-year evidence | ruler attribution: Putin, parliament, and the conservative policy bloc | inherited/context limits: this is a legal-policy source, not a physical-violence report | contrary considerations: the law is not framed as violent in itself, but it materially increases vulnerability and state coercion | lenses: 3B.3, 3B.5, 3B.7

- `3B-S095` [Premeditated, Organized and Impactful: Dating Violence as a Method of Committing Hate Crimes Against LGBTQ People in Russia](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10896-023-00638-z) | Springer / Journal of Family Violence | 2023-09-15 | source type: scholarship | source confidence: high, because it is a peer-reviewed open-access article with a court-rulings dataset and explicit methods/results | final evidence use: structural evidence on anti-LGBTQ violence and state-enabled discrimination | language: en | locator: `turn4view2` lines 56-65 | factual claims: the study built a database of more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ violence cases from court rulings; dating violence was a common method of hate crime; the authors argue state discriminatory policies enabled the pattern | temporal fit: strong background and pattern evidence, though not a 2023-only incident report | ruler attribution: state policy environment, not a single direct order | inherited/context limits: scholarship on a 2010-2020 base, so use as structural context rather than target-year incident proof | contrary considerations: it is not a contemporaneous monitoring report, but it is valuable for identifying the violence mechanism and scale | lenses: 3B.3, 3B.7, 3B.8

**Remaining Gaps**
- Direct evidence of effective civilian oversight, complaint handling, and meaningful remedy is still thin relative to repression evidence.
- Evidence that domestic fear was reduced without replacing it with state fear remains weak.
- Broader protection evidence for women, children, and non-LGBT vulnerable groups is still under-supplied.
- Several official/legal pages in this wave were inaccessible, so the legal-infrastructure record is still incomplete here.
- The accepted pool is now broad enough for chapter drafting, but the weakest lenses remain 3B.4 and 3B.6.
